qs.q: What is the primary pathological consequence and risk associated with untreated vesicoureteral reflux in children?
o: Progressive pyelonephritis leading to loss of renal function
Rapid onset of bladder exstrophy at birth
Widespread mucosal calcification resulting in stone formation
Conversion to squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary tract
qs.e: Vesicoureteral reflux is the most serious congenital anomaly of the bladder because it predisposes the patient to ascending pyelonephritis and subsequent loss of renal function. It does not directly cause bladder exstrophy, which is a separate structural wall defect.

qs.q: A voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) is performed on a 2-year-old girl with pyelonephritis, demonstrating contrast reflux into the ureter and renal pelvis with mild dilation and well-preserved caliceal fornices. Which grade of vesicoureteral reflux does this represent?
qs.e: Grade III VUR is defined by mild dilation of the renal pelvis and ureter without the loss of calyces. Grade II shows no dilation, Grade IV has moderate dilation with loss of calyces, and Grade V shows severe dilation with tortuosity.

qs.q: What radionuclide scan is used in the surveillance of vesicoureteral reflux to assess renal morphology, structure, and function?
qs.e: A DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan is a radionuclide scan utilized to assess renal morphology, structure, and function in patients undergoing conservative management for VUR. It helps detect renal scarring.

qs.q: Which diagnostic modality is considered the gold standard to rule out vesicoureteral reflux (VUR)?
qs.e: Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) uses contrast in the urinary tract to diagnose and grade vesicoureteral reflux. Ultrasound is the initial imaging study for urinary tract anomalies but MCUG rules out VUR.

qs.q: An 18-month-old girl with recurrent febrile urinary tract infections is diagnosed with low-grade vesicoureteral reflux. What is the recommended initial conservative medical management?
o: Continuous systemic corticosteroid therapy during peak infection seasons
High-dose therapeutic broad-spectrum antibiotics for six continuous months
Prophylactic antibiotics given once daily at a fraction of the full dose
Long-acting urinary alkalinizers taken three times daily after meals
qs.e: Management includes prophylactic antibiotics given once a day at 1/3 of the therapeutic dose, choosing an agent that concentrates in the urine. Surgical treatment is reserved for breakthrough infections or high grades.

qs.q: A voiding cystourethrogram is performed on a 3-year-old boy to investigate recurrent urinary tract infections, revealing contrast reflux into the renal pelvis with mild calyceal blunting. How is this grade of vesicoureteral reflux classified?
o: Severe tortuosity and massive dilation of the entire collecting system
Contrast confined strictly to the distal ureter without reaching the pelvis
Reflux into the collecting system with complete effacement of all calyces
Mild dilation of the renal pelvis and ureter without loss of calyces
qs.e: Grade III VUR represents mild dilation of the renal pelvis and ureter without loss of calyces. Grade V features severe dilation and a tortuous ureter.

qs.q: A 3-year-old girl with grade III vesicoureteral reflux and continuous antibiotic prophylaxis is evaluated in the clinic. Which finding serves as a definitive indication for surgical ureteral reimplantation?
qs.e: Breakthrough febrile urinary tract infections while compliant with prophylactic antibiotics are a primary indication for surgical ureteral reimplantation. Stable low-grade reflux without infection is managed medically with observation.
